# Intended Audience
The intended audience is Parkinson's researchers and clinical data scientists who specialize in motor scoring and patient phenotyping.

# Design Rational

The poster’s red color palette and warm tones convey clinical urgency while being symbolic towards Parkinson's awareness as the disease is symbolised by a red tulip. A composite graphic—incorporating a brain, gears, and lightning bolts—visually summarizes the study’s focus. The gear represents motor function, while the caution sign and lightning bolts emphasize the neurological disruption inherent in the disease.
The layout follows a logical zigzag hierarchy, moving from foundational distributions in the top left to complex multivariate results. This structure ensures viewers grasp demographic context before interpreting primary phenotypic findings. To ensure readability for researchers, trend and contour lines utilize a light pink underlay beneath black to enhance contrast without breaking the established color scheme.
The design is specifically tailored for an expert audience of biostatisticians and Parkinson’s researchers. By assuming a baseline proficiency with the MDS-UPDRS scale and clinical phenotyping, I intentionally avoided redundant explanations of standard motor terminology or basic statistical values. This allowed the focus to remain on nuanced relationships and the "directional" interpretation of the data. For the PCA biplot, I prioritized visualizing symptom divergence over raw coordinate values, trusting the audience to interpret the loading vectors and variance distributions independently.
This high-level approach is supplemented by a QR code linking to an interactive visualization, enabling peers to conduct granular data exploration. Captions remain concise, focusing on observable patterns, while key insights provide deeper interpretation. Together, these choices balance immediate visual impact with the technical rigor required for a specialized clinical environment.

```{r motor_cog_scatter, echo=FALSE}
# =========================================
# MOTOR vs COGNITION HEAT-SCATTER PLOT
# =========================================

# 1. Create the high-contrast heat-scatter plot
p <- ggplot(df_moca_final, aes(x = NP3TOT, y = MCATOT)) +
  
  # Point density layer (with jitter to reduce overplotting)
  geom_pointdensity(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0.3),
    adjust = 3,
    size = 1
  ) +
  
  # Restrict x-axis range
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 80)) +
  
  # Custom high-contrast density color scale
  scale_color_gradientn(
    colors = c(
      "#3B0000", "#7A0000", "#B30000",
      "#E60000", "#FF4D00", "#FF9900", "#FFD700"
    ),
    name = "Patient Density"
  ) +
  
  # Density contour lines (white underlay + black overlay for contrast)
  geom_density_2d(color = "white", linewidth = 1.7, alpha = 1) +
  geom_density_2d(color = "black", linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 1) +
  
  # Linear trend line (highlight + outline for visibility)
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "pink", linewidth = 2, se = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#1A1A1A", linewidth = 1.4, se = TRUE) +
  
  # Labels
  labs(
    title = "Motor Severity vs Cognitive Function",
    x = "Motor Severity (NP3 Total Score)",
    y = "Cognitive Score (MoCA Total)"
  ) +
  
  # Base theme
  theme_minimal() +
  
  # Custom styling
  theme(
    # Remove grid and background clutter
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_blank(),
    
    # Add clear axis lines
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
    
    # Legend formatting
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "horizontal",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 28),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 22),
    
    # Plot background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Title formatting
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 42,
      face = "bold",
      hjust = 0.5
    ),
    
    # Axis labels and ticks
    axis.title = element_text(size = 34),
    axis.text  = element_text(size = 30)
  ) +
  
  # Force horizontal colorbar
  guides(
    color = guide_colorbar(
      title.position = "top",
      barwidth = 25
    )
  )

#2. Save plot as SVG
ggsave(
  filename = "motor_severity_cog_scatter.svg", 
  plot = p,
  width = 7.1,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  scale = 2
)

# 3. Display plot
print(p)
```

```{r corr_heatmap, echo=FALSE}
# =========================================
# CORRELATION HEATMAP: MOTOR SYMPTOMS
# =========================================

# 1. Select and rename variables for readability
df_corr <- df_clean_final %>%
  select(all_of(np3_vars)) %>%
  rename(
    `Postural Tremor of RH` = NP3PTRMR,
    `Postural Tremor of LH` = NP3PTRML,
    `Kinetic Tremor of RH` = NP3KTRMR,
    `Kinetic Tremor of LH` = NP3KTRML,
    `Rigidity of neck` = NP3RIGN,
    `Rigidity of RUE` = NP3RIGRU,
    `Rigidity of LUE` = NP3RIGLU,
    `Body Bradykinesia` = NP3BRADY,
    `Finger Taps, RH` = NP3FTAPR,
    `Finger Taps, LH` = NP3FTAPL,
    Gait = NP3GAIT,
    `Postural Stability` = NP3PSTBL,
    Speech = NP3SPCH,
    `Facial Expression` = NP3FACXP
  )

# 2. Compute Spearman correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(
  df_corr,
  use = "complete.obs",
  method = "spearman"
)

# 3. Hierarchical clustering for ordering
hc <- hclust(as.dist(1 - abs(cor_matrix)))
cor_matrix_ord <- cor_matrix[hc$order, hc$order]

# 4. Convert matrix to long format
cor_df <- as.data.frame(cor_matrix_ord) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Var1,
    names_to = "Var2",
    values_to = "value"
  )

# 5. Remove diagonal + duplicate pairs
cor_df <- cor_df %>%
  filter(Var1 != Var2) %>%
  mutate(
    Var1 = factor(Var1, levels = rownames(cor_matrix_ord)),
    Var2 = factor(Var2, levels = colnames(cor_matrix_ord))
  ) %>%
  filter(as.numeric(Var1) < as.numeric(Var2))

# 6. Scaling reference values
min_val <- min(cor_df$value, na.rm = TRUE)
max_abs <- max(abs(cor_df$value), na.rm = TRUE)

# 7. Plot correlation heatmap
p_corr <- ggplot(cor_df, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = value)) +
  
  # Heatmap tiles
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  
  # Diverging colour scale
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(0, max_abs)
  ) +
  
  # Square layout
  coord_fixed() +
  
  # Base theme
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  
  # Styling
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1,
      vjust = 1,
      size = 11,
      margin = margin(t = 10, r = 6)
    ),
    
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12),
    
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 22,
      face = "bold",
      hjust = 0.5
    ),
    
    legend.title = element_text(size = 13),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
    
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Between Motor Symptoms",
    x = "",
    y = "",
    fill = "Correlation"
  )

# 8. Display plot
print(p_corr)

# 9. Save plot
ggsave(
  filename = "Age_vs_Motor_Heatscatter.svg",
  plot = p_corr,
  device = "svg",
  width = 6.7,
  height = 6.1,
  units = "in"
)
```

```{r np3_pca, echo=FALSE}

# =========================================
# PCA: MOTOR SYMPTOM STRUCTURE ANALYSIS
# =========================================

# -------------------------
# 1. PCA PREPARATION
# -------------------------

# Select motor symptom variables and remove missing values
pca_data <- df_clean_final %>%
  select(all_of(np3_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

# Run PCA with scaling
pca_res <- prcomp(pca_data, scale. = TRUE)

# -------------------------
# 2. EXPLORATORY OUTPUT
# -------------------------

# Scree plot (variance explained per component)
plot(pca_res, type = "l", main = "Scree Plot")

# PCA scores (patient-level coordinates in PC space)
pca_df <- as.data.frame(pca_res$x)

# Loadings (variable contributions to PCs)
loadings <- as.data.frame(pca_res$rotation)
loadings$Feature <- rownames(loadings)

# Optional scaling factor (for vector plots if needed later)
scaling_factor <- 8

# -------------------------
# 3. PCA VISUALISATION
# -------------------------

# Create PCA scatter plot with density overlay
p_pca <- ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  
  # Density-based point colouring
  geom_pointdensity(adjust = 3, size = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  
  # Density colour scale
  scale_color_gradientn(
    colors = c(
      "#3B0000", "#E60000",
      "#FF4D00", "#FF9900", "#FFD700"
    ),
    name = "Density"
  ) +
  
  # Labels
  labs(
    title = "Clinical Patterns of Motor Symptoms",
    x = "PC1 (Overall Motor Severity)",
    y = "PC2 (Tremor Severity)"
  ) +
  
  # Base theme
  theme_minimal() +
  
  # Custom styling
  theme(
    # Remove grid lines
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
    # Axis structure
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 22,
      face = "bold",
      hjust = 0.5
    ),
    
    # Axis labels
    axis.title = element_text(size = 18),
    
    # Axis tick labels
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.title = element_text(size = 13),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
    
    # Background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )

# -------------------------
# 4. SAVE OUTPUT
# -------------------------

ggsave(
  filename = "np3_PCA.svg",
  plot = p_pca,
  device = "svg",
  width = 14.7,
  height = 9.6,
  units = "in"
)

# Display PCA plot
print(p_pca)

# -------------------------
# 5. PCA FEATURE INSIGHTS
# -------------------------

# Top contributing features for PC1 and PC2
loadings %>%
  select(Feature, PC1, PC2) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(PC1, PC2),
    names_to = "PC",
    values_to = "Weight"
  ) %>%
  group_by(PC) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = abs(Weight), n = 5) %>%
  arrange(PC, desc(Weight))

# Full loading matrix inspection
print(pca_res$rotation[, 1:2])
```
